threats.rationale: Use after free needs manual deallocation. Dart has none; the escape routes are dart:ffi (Pointer, malloc.free, a NativeFinalizer) and native extensions. The package imports nothing outside itself (gates.dart has no import; combinational.dart:1 and sequential.dart:1 import only ./gates.dart), so the escape routes (dart:ffi pointers, native extensions, external memory behind typed data) are absent; that the package stays inside that subset is read by a person today, and the analyzer rule is planned (LGE-A-DART). Excluded by the registry subset gc_runtimes only when the FFI-free rule is live. VM and compiler bugs are outside the package.

threats.name: Integer Overflow to Buffer Boundary
threats.rationale: The registry class is wraparound that leads to a wrong buffer size or offset. Dart ints are 64-bit on the VM (wrap silently on overflow and on a left shift of 64 or more) and doubles with integer semantics on the web (bitwise operators and shifts are 32-bit). The basic gates do one subtraction on a validated bit (1 - a, gates.dart:28) and cannot wrap. The combinational block sizes allocations with a shift of a caller-controlled length (1 << select.length at combinational.dart:36, 1 << inputs.length at :63) and builds an index with bit << index (:132): this is exactly wrap-to-size, measured locally on 2026-11-24: decoder of 64 zero bits returns an empty list on the VM, decoder of 32 zero bits does on dart2js. That is a finding in a sibling module (see dart.vm-shift-and-width-wrap and dart.unreviewed-sibling-modules). The exclusion rules scan lib/**, so an excluded status would cover the siblings too, and this row stays open until the range rule and the caps exist and the siblings are covered by them. threats.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
threats.rationale: The two-input gates are constant time. andN, orN and xorN take a caller List of any length and loop over it (gates.dart:102-132): linear work that is unbounded: no length cap, and the loops re-read inputs.length on every iteration (xorN :114, _requireAtLeastTwo :129), so a List whose length keeps growing never terminates (dart.length-reread-unbounded-loop). They are not allocation-free on valid input: _requireAtLeastTwo and xorN build an inputs[$index] String for every element before validateBit looks at the value (gates.dart:115, 130), and skip(1).fold allocates an iterable and calls a closure per element (:104, 109, 118). On invalid input the error message is built from a literal and an int, and the List is passed to ArgumentError.value, which prints it safely as Instance of ... (observed locally on Dart 3.13.4, 2026-11-24: a caller List subclass with an overriding toString was not called). The combinational and sequential blocks are worse: decoder and demux allocate 2^n entries for n caller bits with no cap (combinational.dart:36,47,62-65) and the register, shift register and counter allocate caller-width lists (sequential.dart:124-135,158,190); a width too large for the heap ends in OutOfMemoryError, an Error that is not an ArgumentError. The registry route pure_zero_allocation cannot hold for the package: decoder, demux and the register functions must allocate their outputs, so, as in the TypeScript lane, the row has no exclusion route and carries cannot_close_in_package; the exclusion rules scan lib/**, so the siblings would be covered too, and the row stays open until they are. The package-local fix for the gates (read length once, read each index once, build the name only on failure, cap the length with a bound test) is planned and supporting only. The discharge route (microbenchmark, step-bound proof, input-bound rejection) stays unavailable: no benchmark harness or proof tool exists for dart. threats.name: Caller List subclass: length and [] run caller code and can change between reads
threats.rationale: andN, orN, xorN, mux4, mux8, muxN, demux, decoder, encoder, priorityEncoder, register and the sequential functions take a List<int>, and List is an interface a caller can implement (ListBase, a view, a lazy generator): length and [] are caller code, they can return different answers each call, and an infinite or enormous length can be claimed.
